newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak analysts wary of slowdown in M2 growth.
newsitem.headline: Slovak analysts wary of slowdown in M2 growth.

text.p: The key Slovak money supply measure, M2, rose 19.5 percent year-on-year in August, compared with 21.0 percent growth in July, the National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) said on Friday.
Analysts wondered whether the modest slowdown in M2 growth would hold, and whether it happened for the right reasons.
"M2 slowed down, but for a bad reason. The net foreign asset contribution to the money supply declined," a western banker who requested anonymity told Reuters.
Net foreign assets totalled 59.1 billion crowns in August, up 10.5 billion from August 1995, after 12-month growth of 13.7 billion crowns in July.
Growth in net domestic assets rose 50.9 billion crowns to 317.2 billion crowns in August, after a 50.8 billion crown 12-month increase in July.

In mid-July, the NBS approved a series of measures aimed at slowing money supply growth, including raising banks' minimum reserve levels and a key lending rate, and widening the band in which it fixes the crown to scare off speculative hot money.
The move was aimed at curbing short-term lending by local banks, which is at the heart of M2 growth.
Local banks have been repatriating their assets from abroad to have funds to extend the loans to "lucrative Slovak clients", increasingly also in foreign exchange.
"The aggregate growth moderated only slightly and, as a one-month phenomenon, one should wait at least for another month to assess the decline's roots," said Martin Barto, an ING Barings analyst.

But the NBS, which had said it expected the first reliable results of the measures in October or by end-year, took further steps on Thursday to push banks to buy its three-month liquidity bills, its main tightening tool.
The NBS raised its bill repurchase rate by 50 basis points to 8.70 percent, and also cut its reverse repo rate by 20 basis points to 7.20 percent on Thursday.

"The NBS cautiousness is justified, loosening of monetary policy is fine in a country where restructuring is guaranteed, but this is not the case in Slovakia," Juraj Rencko, an independent economist, told Reuters.
"Contrary to the Czech Republic, the loan expansion in Slovakia is taking place despite low foreign capital inflow," Rencko added.
